chat:
The gazetteer is three files:

**`gazetteer_sites.csv`** — 36 verified sites: 15 with precisely sourced coordinates (Huaca Prieta, Chan Chan, Sipán, Túcume, Ingapirca, Cochasquí, the Upano Valley cluster, and more), the rest with coordinates deliberately left blank and flagged for proper geocoding rather than estimated. It folds in the major type-sites the chronology had only named as cultures — Kuélap for Chachapoya, Chan Chan for Chimú, Sipán/Túcume/Batán Grande for Moche/Sicán — plus every founding city, battle site, and border zone from the earlier work.

**`gazetteer_disputed_narratives.csv`** — kept structurally separate from the main table, for the same reason the hemispheric comparanda stayed separate from the periods table: these are a different kind of evidence and would corrupt a GIS layer if mixed in. Three cases, three different flavors of "disputed":
- The **Reino de Quito / Shyris dynasty** — a whole pre-Inca kingdom that appears in exactly one 18th-century source and was formally struck from Ecuadorian school curricula in 1918, still repeated as fact in places today
- **Cueva de los Tayos** — a real, mappable cave with a "metal library" claim its own promoter's collaborator admitted was fabricated
- The **Llanganates treasure** — a real national park carrying a 500-year-old unverified gold legend

**`Gazetteer_Methodology.md`** — explains why disputes are split into four types (contested interpretation, contested historicity, pseudo-archaeology attached to a real place, and formal territorial disputes like Cordillera del Cóndor/Tiwinza), the coordinate-confidence tiers, and what's deliberately *not* in here (this is curated from everything surfaced in our conversation, not an exhaustive national inventory — that needs direct INPC/Ministerio de Cultura/ICANH database access I don't have).

One process note: my first pass at writing the CSVs had a quoting bug — commas inside unquoted fields silently split several rows into the wrong number of columns. I validated with a script before delivering, caught it, and rebuilt both files programmatically to guarantee correct structure. Worth knowing if you round-trip these through QGIS: they're now clean, but it's a reminder to validate row/column counts on any hand-assembled CSV before trusting it downstream.

The atlas is now 9 layers. The core problem with this request was that "organize into GIS-ready layers with symbology" is easy for volcanoes (real coordinates) and dishonest for sea-level/vegetation/glacier data if done carelessly — those are inherently regional claims, not points, and drawing fake polygon boundaries for them would look more authoritative than the evidence supports.

One of those ten points is worth flagging specifically: I went and fetched the actual **PANGAEA dataset record** for the Gulf of Guayaquil pollen core, which gives the exact coring coordinates (-3.7498°, -81.1208°), the research vessel, the collection date, and the water depth straight from the dataset's own metadata. That's a meaningfully different sourcing tier than a Wikipedia infobox, and it now anchors the best-evidenced claim in the whole environmental reconstruction — the three-phase Holocene vegetation sequence.

Every layer got the same symbology treatment as the routes layer from last session: `volcanic_eruptions` sizes points by VEI and color-codes by whether the archaeological link is independently sourced or my own plausible inference (Quilotoa is dark and large; Sangay's Upano-River connection stays light, flagged as inference, same as before). Two loadable `.qml` files mean you don't have to translate any of this into symbology yourself.

One gap stated rather than papered over: EN05 (earliest irrigation canals, Nanchoc Valley) still has no reference point — I didn't find verified coordinates for it this session either, and its `mapping_reference_point_id` field says so explicitly instead of silently joining to nothing.
